output.headline: Police hold far-right activist Daniel Thomas on suspicion of endangering life two days after Channel dinghy slashed
output.bodyHtml:
Police have arrested Daniel Thomas, the far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist, on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life, two days after he filmed himself slashing the side of a dinghy in the middle of the Channel while a rescuer was on board.

In a statement, Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said a 37-year-old man, of no fixed abode, had been arrested on Wednesday night “on suspicion of destroying ships or fixed platforms or endangering their safety under section 11 of the Aviation and Maritime Security Act 1990”.

Officers also suspect Thomas of “criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life, and conduct endangering ships, structures or individuals under section 58 of the Merchant Shipping Act 1995”, the police said.

The arrest on Wednesday night appears to have been filmed by Thomas himself. A video uploaded on to his YouTube platform shows the arrest, apparently at a garage, and an officer telling him he had been “involved in criminal damage that has recklessly endangered someone’s life”.

Thomas, who prefers to go by the name Danny Tommo, said: “I understand. I knew this was coming.”

Over the summer Thomas has brought dozens of nationalist protest groups together under the umbrella movement Patriot Platform.

He was also behind this month’s anti-immigration marches by masked men in Dover and Portsmouth.

More details soon …
output.standfirst: Thirty-seven-year-old arrested on Wednesday night on suspicion of crimes including criminal damage with intent to endanger life, two days after he filmed himself cutting a dinghy while a rescuer was on board

output.headline: Andy Burnham makes case for trial to lift ban on alcohol in football stands
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham has set out a case for lifting the ban on drinking alcohol in the stands at football matches, signalling he may end it and suggesting it is “unfair” for fans to be singled out when it is permitted for other sports.

The prime minister, a committed Everton fan who still attends matches, said an end to the ban could be trialled to bring football in line with rugby and cricket.

The Football Supporters’ Association and the English Football League welcomed the move, and police said the impact on safety should be considered first, warning it would be “incredibly rash” to make changes without doing so.

Burnham has long opposed the ban, arguing it is discriminatory and out of date, harking back to an era when football violence was fuelled by drinking within view of the pitch.

Speaking to reporters on the plane to New York, Burnham was asked about lifting a ban and said: “I don’t think it’s fair for football fans to be singled out in that way and I made that point. I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different. And I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination.

“There are different ways it could be done, perhaps on a trial basis. But I’m not going to back away from what’s been a long-held view of mine. I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently.”

In England and Wales, drinking in sight of the pitch is prohibited by the Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol etc) Act 1985.

A re-examination of the ban was already called for by the fan-led review of football governance in 2021, which suggested piloting the sale of alcohol within sight of the pitch in lower-tier English football.

The UK Football Policing Unit, which coordinates football policing policy in England and Wales, offered to meet the prime minister. A spokesperson said: “The UKFPU would welcome a meeting with the prime minister to discuss his views and explain the challenges these proposed changes would bring to policing and the safety of staff and fans at football games.

“Other sports simply don’t see the violence and criminal behaviour from their supporters that football does, albeit a minority, with alcohol often playing a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour. It would be irresponsible to fuel this by allowing greater alcohol consumption during games.

“Following a number of football-related tragedies, changes in legislation were implemented after the Taylor report [of 1990 into the causes of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster] for good reason and we are currently in the longest ever period without a significant football-related disaster. It would be incredibly rash to make fundamental changes without a full examination of the evidence and meaningful consultation with police practitioners who have the expertise in this area.”

The English Football League said it would be “receptive” to a review of legislation that “was introduced more than 40 years ago and has not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding”, a spokesperson said.

Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters’ Association, welcomed the comments. He said: “The FSA has always argued that it’s unfair to criminalise football fans for having a pint while watching the match – especially since you can sit in the same seat drinking alcohol whilst watching an Oasis gig or rugby league. We welcome the prime minister’s comments and totally agree that the legislation is outdated and deserves to be reviewed. We look forward to being part of that consultation.”

A successful 18-month trial has already led to a change in the women’s game: supporters at Women’s Super League and WSL2 matches have been permitted to drink alcohol in view of the pitch since the start of this season, after the WSL changed its regulations this summer to allow clubs – but not oblige them – to give fans that option.

Since that rule change, 25 of the 26 clubs across the two divisions of English women’s football have decided to take up the option at all of their home games. Brighton & Hove Albion’s home matches at Crawley’s Broadfield Stadium are the only exception, and Brighton have permitted fans to drink in view of the pitch when the team play their home matches at the Amex Stadium, such as last Sunday when they hosted Aston Villa. Women’s matches have typically seen fewer incidents of crowd trouble.
output.standfirst: Prime minister says the measure is discriminatory when fans of other sports are not similarly restricted, as supporters’ groups and the EFL welcome a review and police seek a meeting on safety

output.headline: Better blood pressure detection could help tens of thousands avoid heart attacks and strokes, says British Heart Foundation
output.bodyHtml:
Better detection and treatment of high blood pressure could help tens of thousands of people avoid a preventable heart attack or stroke, the British Heart Foundation says, in response to research revealing that only half of people being treated by a GP for the condition in England have it under control, and that millions more are completely unaware they have the ‘silent killer’ condition.

The largest ever study of its kind has now established that most people with hypertension (59 per cent) are undiagnosed and in the dark, which raises their risk of stroke, heart attack and early death.

The Oxford University study of 1.4 million adults suggests that even among those who are diagnosed and receiving medication via their family doctor, blood pressure is out of control in 50 per cent of cases.

The researchers, whose findings are published in the journal BMJ Public Health, said they suggested the current approach to detecting and treating high blood pressure in England was ‘not fit for purpose’.

The study drew on data from the Our Future Health programme, examining people enrolled between 2022 and 2025 who had high blood pressure, defined as 140/90 mmHg or higher.

Related: ‘People should not feel guilty’: weekend lie-in may be good for you, experts say

The researchers were able to calculate that more than a third of adults (37 per cent) had high blood pressure, and that six in 10 of these were oblivious to their condition.

The research also pinpointed who is most affected: hypertension was almost 50 per cent more common in men than women (42 per cent compared with 29 per cent across all ages), and more common in older people.

Detection and control of high blood pressure improved substantially during the 2000s, the researchers said, though progress had plateaued since about 2011.

The researchers also identified ‘indications of worsening trends following the Covid-19 pandemic, possibly because disruptions to healthcare delivery may have had lasting effects’.

Wenyu Liu, a medical statistician at Oxford Population Health and lead author of the study, said: ‘While hypertension is largely a “silent killer”, the current approach to detecting and treating high blood pressure is not fit for purpose.

‘Our study highlights the prevalence of hypertension across demographics. This underscores the need for population-wide prevention strategies alongside targeted treatment for people at high cardiovascular risk.’

The researchers singled out ‘the most striking finding’ of the study as the high absolute number and the high proportion of people with undiagnosed hypertension. The study also found that only half of adults with high blood pressure treated by a GP were adequately controlled.

Dr Iain Turnbull, a GP, deputy chief medical officer at Our Future Health and a clinical research fellow at Oxford Population Health, set out the possible explanations for that figure, saying it was not clear why 50 per cent of patients who said they were taking blood pressure-lowering drugs had uncontrolled hypertension.

‘Blood pressure varies considerably between people, and some people need changes in dose or two or more different medicines before it is brought under control. Other health conditions and medications can affect blood pressure, too.

Related: AI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggests

‘There are also practical and social factors: side effects, complicated treatment regimens and competing health or life pressures can make medicines difficult to take consistently. Weight, diet, salt intake, alcohol and physical activity can also influence blood pressure.

‘So a high reading can have many explanations and shouldn’t be seen simply as a reflection of what an individual patient or healthcare professional has done.

‘There are also some important caveats … we did not have prescribing records available to independently confirm medication use, and a blood pressure measurement on one day does not necessarily represent someone’s usual blood pressure.

‘Even with those caveats, I wouldn’t regard 50 per cent as a satisfactory figure. Persistently high blood pressure increases the risk of stroke and heart disease, and bringing it under control reduces that risk.’

Prof Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, set out what he believes better detection could achieve, while saying the study ‘paints a concerning picture of the scale of undetected high blood pressure in the UK, and the challenges of keeping blood pressure under control in those already receiving treatment’.

He added: ‘Better detection and treatment could help tens of thousands of people to avoid a preventable heart attack and stroke. But to achieve this, we will need to rethink how we identify, treat and support those at risk so that blood pressure checks and effective treatment can benefit everyone.’
output.standfirst: Largest study of its kind finds 59 per cent of cases in England undiagnosed and current approach ‘not fit for purpose’, with researchers calling for population-wide prevention

output.headline: Judge orders White House to restore access for CNN, MS Now and Politico, finding ban likely unconstitutional
output.bodyHtml:
Journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico are to have their White House access temporarily restored after a federal judge ruled that the president’s ban on the three media outlets was likely unconstitutional and ordered the Trump administration to reinstate them.

US district judge Tim Kelly made his order in a lawsuit brought by the news organisations to contest the ban, which the president announced on 18 September.

Kelly’s temporary restraining order, which will be in effect for 14 days, requires the Trump administration to return the outlets’ press passes immediately. Orders of this kind are typically designed to preserve the status quo while the court reviews the case more closely.

Related: DoJ defends Trump media ban: ‘Access to the White House is a privilege’

Earlier on Wednesday Kelly set out past case law that clearly established the need for a distinct process, one involving advance notice of an infraction and the opportunity to plead one’s case.

Prior cases, the judge said, made clear that ‘before a journalist’s White House hard pass was suspended or revoked, that the journalist was entitled to pre-deprivation notice and an opportunity to be heard’.

The judge signalled scepticism when a Justice Department lawyer told him the Trump administration had given a sufficient explanation for the revocation of the press passes in letters sent to the news outlets on Tuesday, noting that the letters were sent after the revocation occurred and the lawsuit was filed.

Trump had said on social media that the three outlets ‘shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES’, and justice department lawyers had sought to justify the ban on national security grounds.

The three outlets had sued Trump and other members of his administration in federal court in Washington on Monday, arguing that the ban violated the US constitution’s first amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. They asked for a temporary restraining order that would immediately reinstate their White House access while their legal challenge plays out.

The Justice Department, in a legal filing on Tuesday, argued that access to the White House is a privilege, not an entitlement, and that the president has the authority to suspend access by news organisations.

A coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organisations lent their support to the three outlets in a legal brief filed on Wednesday, asserting that ‘stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of supreme court jurisprudence’.

The brief’s signatories included the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, Reuters, the Washington Post and Fox News, among others.

With Reuters and the Associated Press
output.standfirst: US district judge Tim Kelly issues 14-day temporary restraining order returning the outlets’ press passes pending closer review, after the president announced his ban on 18 September

output.headline: Miliband pledges £330m and climate security taskforce as UK shares findings of report suppressed under Starmer
output.bodyHtml:
The UK is to appoint a special representative for climate security, set up a ministerial taskforce and put £330m into protecting nature, after warning countries around the world that the climate and nature crises and the coming El Niño threaten their national security and defence, presenting foreign ministries with the findings of a report suppressed under Keir Starmer.

Ed Miliband, the UK’s foreign secretary, presented the findings to the foreign ministers of the EU as well as Kenya and other countries at a private meeting on Wednesday night during the UN general assembly in New York. His presentation drew on the report by the UK’s spy chiefs, which established that the collapse of natural systems around the world would lead to conflict, migration and food shortages.

The meeting was the first such discussion among foreign ministers. Miliband told it that the coming El Niño, which has been supercharged by climate breakdown, would test the world’s food systems as never before.

“We face an El Niño that is already set to be the most intense in living memory,” he said. “This will intensify climate shocks that compound and cascade across borders, threatening food and water security, displacing communities, putting pressure on markets and scarring economies.”

Governments must deal with this at the highest levels, he said, and this year’s heatwaves, bad harvests and food price inflation had shown them what they were in for.

“Climate change and nature loss have never been issues for climate and environment ministers alone,” he said. “They are defining challenges for our citizens, our economies, our foreign policy and our national security.”

Miliband presented the research with the backing of Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister. It found that the collapse of global ecosystems such as the Amazon and Congo rainforests, driven by the climate crisis and the destruction of nature, would have impacts on national security around the world.

The joint intelligence committee (JIC) report, revealed by the Guardian, is partly in the public domain: a redacted version was issued in January under the Freedom of Information Act, after Downing Street suppressed the report on the eve of its launch, which had been scheduled for last October. Ministers have continued to resist calls for the full report to be made public.

Richard Nugee, a retired general and security expert, told the Guardian that governments must treat the climate as they would other threats to national security, such as sabotage by hostile states.

“If a bridge is washed away, it has the same impact whether it’s done by [a foreign power] or the climate,” he said. “The climate crisis will affect food security, energy security, water security, and lead to migration and potentially the recruitment of farmers to [terrorist organisations such as] Isis. Countries should absolutely be treating this as a national security issue.”

It was “very rare” for security reports to be published, he said, so it was not surprising that the JIC report had been suppressed and redacted.

Miliband will appoint a new special representative for climate security and set up a new ministerial taskforce on “the national security and resilience risks of a changing climate and nature loss”, bringing together military and security experts as well as climate scientists.

He also announced £330m for the Global Environment Facility, the main international fund for protecting nature, to go towards protecting forests, oceans and other critical ecosystems in developing countries.

The closed-door meeting among foreign ministers followed a public speech Miliband made on Monday at the UN general assembly that touched on the links between the climate and national security. The former energy secretary had told the Guardian soon after taking office in July that he would put the climate at the heart of UK foreign policy.

On Wednesday night, Miliband said: “The countries fit for the future will be those that see climate and nature as intrinsic to economic and national security. Countries that anticipate risks and invest in resilience before crises hit.

“Countries that seize the incredible opportunities the clean energy transition presents. Countries that don’t just see the connections but act on them.”

He added: “That is why the UK is placing climate and nature security at the heart of our national security and foreign policy decision-making.”

Adrian Ramsay, the Green party MP for Waveney Valley, has campaigned for the JIC report to be made public. He said: “It’s good that the foreign secretary is presenting the findings of this crucial report to ministers from other governments.

“But it begs the question, why are MPs in this country still being denied access to the full report? And, most importantly, why has our government still not published its response to how it will address the stark findings?”
output.standfirst: Foreign secretary tells first such meeting of foreign ministers at UN that El Niño poses critical threat to nations’ defences, and sets out UK’s response

output.headline: Netanyahu to set out ‘what still should be done’ in UN speech, envoy says, as protests and walkout are planned
output.bodyHtml:
Benjamin Netanyahu will use his UN speech on Thursday to “highlight Israel’s achievements” and set out “what still should be done” in the war, according to Israel’s ambassador to the UN, delivering a familiar message of defiance even as protests and international condemnation leave the Israeli leader in growing isolation.

Israeli voters go to the polls in October, and Netanyahu is facing his toughest re-election challenge in a political career spanning decades, with three ongoing conflicts in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran and a growing campaign of violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.

The UK, France and Canada are planning to sanction Israeli settlements in the West Bank, part of growing international condemnation of Israel, and the British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has accused Israeli settlers of committing ethnic cleansing of Palestinian communities.

American opinion is moving too: 62% of respondents told Pew in July they had a negative opinion of Netanyahu’s government, and 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week hope he is voted out in October, in what amounts to a historic shift in US public opinion against Israel.

New York City’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, assured demonstrators this week that he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city”, tempering his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal, as protests are expected both in the UN’s general assembly hall and on the city’s streets.

Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, set out the government’s case in a telephone interview before this week’s speech, defending Netanyahu’s government and seeking to cast criticism of Israel’s actions as the product of misinformation and bias.

“We are aware of the fact that we had a very challenging three years since October 7,” Danon said. “We accomplished a lot, but we were criticised. We were under the spotlight, and for us, I think, we are proud of our achievements.”

He added: “At the same time, we will work harder to improve the image of Israel, and we know there’s a campaign against us.”

Organisers have scheduled several protests in New York City on Thursday, where anger at Netanyahu will be on full display, including one running from Bryant Park in midtown Manhattan to the UN headquarters in Turtle Bay to “reject war criminal Benjamin Netanyahu and the genocidal Zionist project”.

Beth Miller, the political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, said: “Netanyahu is coming to New York amid a political environment that has made it crystal clear that he is not welcome here.”

Public opinion, she said, had seen a “mainstreaming” of the view that “Americans do not want to be supporting Israel’s genocide. We do not want to be supporting Israel’s apartheid. We do not want to be arming Israel or supporting Israel.”

Palestinian representatives, meanwhile, are calling on diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech, to “send a clear message to Netanyahu and his government that no one is willing to aid, abet, or be complicit in its genocide and war crimes and illegal occupation, which all peace-loving states and peoples demand must come to an end”.

Netanyahu would use his speech to “highlight Israel’s achievements”, Danon said, and to lay out “what still should be done, and how should we verify that we actually achieve the goals of the war?” In Danon’s telling, Israel’s problem was largely one of public relations rather than of policy, and he cited a “wave of misinformation” as the reason for the precipitous shift in polling.

The White House and US policymakers will be listening as they calibrate their message to voters – as well as the backlash of public anger – ahead of the upcoming midterm elections, though Danon did not elaborate on those specific measures before the speech.

Netanyahu’s audience, ahead of the October elections, is expected to be his own electorate in Israel as much as world leaders, and his message is expected to be a hardline one. “I think that he is trying to demonstrate to the Israeli populace that he still maintains some level of control over the situation,” Miller said. “And I think that he is trying to speak to a rightwing audience and a Trump-Maga audience in this country to try to rile up the hatred and Islamophobia.”

Netanyahu’s visit is expected to last less than 24 hours, and Donald Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet with him. Trump will be in Washington DC to host the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, and Netanyahu has cited Israel’s electoral campaign and the holiday of Sukkot as his reason to head home quickly after the speech.

Netanyahu’s delegation had sought a high-level meeting during the visit, a Trump administration official said, but none was organised. Danon said there were also no plans to meet congressional leaders.

Israel could face a 2028 campaign with two candidates who no longer support arms sales to Israel or the broad diplomatic support that it has enjoyed in the past, given criticism from top Republicans, including the vice-president, JD Vance, and leading democratic presidential contenders.

Miller noted fractures even within the Maga base, with “more and more people who don’t really want to be sending our tax dollars to support the Israeli government”.

On a potential shift in the US-Israeli security relationship, Danon said: “I think that we are still sharing the same values, and that’s why I’m sure that we will continue to have the support from the US.”

Both US political parties, as well as the international community, now have multiple flashpoints for anger, including dire humanitarian concerns and the lack of reconstruction in Gaza, the expansion of settlements in the West Bank, and continued conflicts in Lebanon and Iran, where the US has found itself mired in a conflict that has driven up global energy prices.

Israel “hopes that we will see [Hamas’s] disarmament without our involvement”, Danon said, nodding to efforts by the Trump-backed Board of Peace, when asked if a controversial $2.8bn (£2.1bn) arms sale indicated that Israel is preparing to resume its offensive in Gaza. If that does not change, he said, Israel “will do it ourselves”, adding: “We can not leave it forever like that.”

On the West Bank he was equally resolute, saying that Israel would not be swayed by recent criticism led by the UK over plans to expand settlements including E1, the planned construction which would sever East Jerusalem from the rest of the West Bank.

Senate Democrats are introducing a bill on Wednesday to sanction facilitators of the new settlement. Senator Chris Coons, a co-sponsor, said in a statement that “as Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behaviour is unacceptable”.

Protesters were out even before Netanyahu arrived in New York.

Several members of the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter rallied on Wednesday at the city’s John F Kennedy international airport, protesting at weapons and explosive materials destined for the Israeli military being flown out of the airport on commercial aircraft.

Speaking at the event was Aber Kawas, who in November is slated to become the first Palestinian-American elected official in New York state; she later told the Guardian she plans to join many other New Yorkers protesting Netanyahu’s UN speech on Thursday.

She said: “Thousands of people are against his presence in our city.”

Some had hailed Netanyahu’s decision to cut his visit short as a victory, she added, but “the fact that he is coming shows he continues to have a sense of entitlement to be centred on the world stage while being the head architect of a genocide”.
output.standfirst: Ambassador Danny Danon says prime minister will ‘highlight Israel’s achievements’ as protests, international condemnation and his toughest re-election challenge in decades await him

output.headline: Nick Clegg calls for greater AI transparency and focus on known threats over ‘godlike’ fears
output.bodyHtml:
Nick Clegg has said tech bosses should concentrate on known, specific threats from AI and on greater transparency, dismissing fears over AI’s “godlike power to exterminate humanity” as a sign that tech bosses are “breathing their own fumes”.

Cybersecurity, bio-weapons and emotional dependence are the known “specific threats” the former UK deputy prime minister said tech bosses should focus on addressing, rather than the “slightly hand-wavy view that this technology is unavoidably going to develop some godlike power which is going to turn on us and exterminate humanity”.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, he explained his objection: “I think it is perhaps accidentally self-serving, because it sort of implies that we can only be made safe by having everything controlled, in effect, by an oligopoly of a small number of companies, and I think it slightly paralyses the political debate.”

Clegg said he spent “a huge amount of time” with people in the tech industry. He was formerly the president of global affairs at Meta, owns more than 917,000 shares in Nscale, a UK-based datacentre, and is a cofounder of AI startup AMI Labs.

Clegg noted that one person who runs an AI lab said the current discourse was “totally silly”. “They don’t agree amongst themselves at all. Of course, we hear the most apocalyptic voices,” he said.

He went on to describe the culture behind such views: “There is a culture in Silicon Valley – it’s an odd place for those who haven’t been there. It is in many ways the centre of the universe, or at least claiming to shape it. It’s also an oddly parochial place. It’s a strange sort of culture where the engineers can get quite close to the technology and start slightly breathing their own fumes as they wind themselves up into a lather about these things.”

Clegg said there was a case for “tramlines and greater transparency” when asked about the autonomous hack conducted by a group of OpenAI agents on a major real-world company, Hugging Face.

He set out the obstacles: this would be unlikely to happen under a Trump administration, he said, given its competitiveness on AI, and he suspected China’s cooperation would be limited, since the development of AI technologies was viewed as a “national mission” after the country was “cheated out of the Industrial Revolution”.

He saw more room for collaboration elsewhere, adding: “I think there’s a great potential for the big three techno democracies in the world – India, Europe and the US – to collaborate more.”

Clegg urged realism about the UK’s role when asked whether the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, could take a lead on such efforts, noting the UK was not a world leader on AI: “We need to be realistic about what influence we can and cannot exert.”

On other proposed remedies, Clegg set out where he disagreed: a “kill switch” would be unworkable, he said, and closed models, where source code is not made public, were no safer than open source models according to the evidence, so he did not favour only producing them.

The remedy he suggested instead was transparency: “There is a lot that can be done both voluntarily and through regulation, to enforce far greater transparency on the way in which these models are concocted and how they operate.”
output.standfirst:
Former deputy PM now involved in tech industry dismisses fears that AI could exterminate humanity, saying many within the sector are ‘winding themselves up into a lather’

  • UK politics live – latest updates

output.headline: US and China extend trade truce to 10 January as Trump greets Xi on the tarmac
output.bodyHtml:
Donald Trump opened Xi Jinping’s state visit to Washington by welcoming the Chinese leader in person on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, an unusual step for a US president, on the same day the two countries agreed to extend their trade truce.

The arrival ceremony that met Xi’s plane was lavish: US service members flanked a 30-metre-long (100ft) red carpet, two B-1 bombers flew overhead in a military flyover and the flags and national anthems of both countries were presented.

Trump and the first lady, Melania, travelled to the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, to shake hands in person with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on Wednesday evening; US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House instead.

Related: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China

Xi’s visit coincides with world leaders gathering in New York for the United Nations general assembly, although the Chinese leader will not address the meeting. He has attended the UNGA just once since becoming president in 2012.

Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group told Reuters: “It’s pretty notable that Xi Jinping is ⁠coming to Washington in the same week as the general assembly, but does not feel bothered to come up to New York. I think a lot of people will say: ‘Where is the real center of decision-making?’”

The US and China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called Busan agreement – a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies – Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced.

The agreement will now run until 10 January, two months after it was due to expire, Bessent told Fox News after meeting the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday.

A formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady and a tour of the National Archives are among the special events that will continue the pageantry.

Trump and Xi will take on many thorny issues over the two-day visit, the simmering trade war among them, along with the race in artificial intelligence development and geopolitical instability.

The White House has invited major tech leaders, such as executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and others, to the state dinner being held for Xi on Thursday.

The carefully orchestrated arrival ceremony had one discordant note: Trump visibly winced at the sound of a US military jet flying overhead as he stood alongside Xi on the red carpet, listening to the US national anthem. Xi remained impassive, as did the wives of both men, while Trump recoiled from the sound of the flyover, video of the moment showed.

A White House livestream captured the moment, which was widely mocked online; Trump’s aides did not include it in the edited highlights of the ceremony they released later.

The race to further AI has become a major topic among tech companies – especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development – within a long-running competition between the US and China to develop increasingly powerful technology.

Trump has promoted more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race, and has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people.

Trump wrote on Truth Social last week: “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so.”

Leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically, the president and members of the administration have insisted – a position that further raises the stakes for the US and China.

Ceremonial displays are expected to fill Xi’s visit, reciprocating the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.

By choosing to greet the Chinese leader at his plane rather than at the White House, the US president showed how far he is willing to go to honour Xi.

“He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump told Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning of the visit, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.”

Robert Mackey contributed reporting
output.standfirst:
Treasury secretary announces extension of ‘Busan agreement’ pausing trade war hostilities as president lays out red carpet for Chinese leader’s state visit

  • AI, trade, Taiwan and climate: what will and won’t be on agenda at Trump-Xi summit
